lessons.title: Scoring choices

lessons.title: Breadth-first search
lessons.objective: Find the shortest way with breadth-first search.

steps.text: Breadth-first search (BFS) explores the closest squares first, so the first time it reaches the goal is the shortest way.
BFS keeps a queue. What does popleft() take?
steps.code:
from collections import deque
q = deque(["near", "far"])
print(q.popleft())
steps.explanation: popleft() takes the oldest item, the one that joined first.

steps.text: A seen set stops the search from visiting a square twice.
steps.code:
seen = {(0, 0)}
print((0, 0) in seen)
seen.add((0, 1))
print(len(seen))

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.code:
start, goal = (0, 0), (0, 3)
print(abs(goal[0] - start[0]) + abs(goal[1] - start[1]))
steps.explanation: On an open grid the shortest way is the row difference plus the column difference: 0 + 3.

steps.text: Breadth-first must take the oldest item from the queue. Fix line 7.
steps.hint: Breadth-first takes from the front: popleft().
steps.explanation: pop() takes the newest item (that is depth-first). BFS takes the oldest with popleft().

steps.text: Print the steps between (1, 1) and (4, 5) on an open grid (7).
steps.hint: Add the row and column differences with abs().

lessons.title: Learning a rule
lessons.objective: Learn a cut-off that separates two groups.

steps.text: A program can learn a rule from examples: put the cut-off halfway between the two groups' averages.
steps.code:
small = [2, 3, 4]
big = [10, 12, 14]
cut = (sum(small) / len(small) + sum(big) / len(big)) / 2
print(cut)

size = 9
print("big" if size > cut else "small")

steps.text: Test the learned rule on new examples.
Type exactly what this prints.
steps.explanation: 5 is not bigger than 5, so it is low.

steps.text: The cut-off is halfway between the two averages. Fix line 3.

b = [9, 11]

lessons.title: Nearest neighbour
lessons.objective: Classify something by the most similar example.

steps.text: Nearest neighbour: a new thing gets the label of the closest known example.
steps.code:
examples = [(1, "small"), (9, "big")]
new = 7
closest = min(examples, key=lambda e: abs(e[0] - new))
print(closest[1])

steps.text: With two features, use the straight-line distance on a grid.

import math
print(math.dist((0, 0), (3, 4)))

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.

steps.text: The nearest example has the smallest distance. Fix line 3.

lessons.title: How accurate?
lessons.objective: Measure how often a model is right.

steps.text: Accuracy is the share of predictions that match the right answers.
steps.code:
predicted = ["cat", "dog", "cat", "dog"]
actual = ["cat", "dog", "dog", "dog"]
right = 0
for p, a in zip(predicted, actual):
    if p == a:
        right = right + 1
print(right / len(actual))

steps.text: What will this print?

steps.text: Show accuracy as a percentage with round().
steps.code:
accuracy = 7 / 9
print(round(accuracy * 100), "%")

steps.text: Type exactly what this prints.
steps.code:

print(right / total * 100)

steps.text: A prediction is right when it matches. Fix line 5.
steps.code:
predicted = ["yes", "no", "yes"]
actual = ["yes", "yes", "yes"]
right = 0
for p, a in zip(predicted, actual):
    if p != a:

steps.explanation: A prediction is right when p == a.
